7:["$","div",null,{"className":"lg:col-span-8","children":[["$","header",null,{"className":"mb-12","children":[["$","h1",null,{"className":"font-serif font-light text-5xl md:text-6xl text-navy mb-4 leading-tight","children":"David Hamilton Jackson"}],["$","div",null,{"className":"w-24 h-[2px] bg-gold"}]]}],["$","section",null,{"className":"prose prose-navy max-w-none","children":[["$","div",null,{"className":"relative mb-12","children":[["$","$L3",null,{"iconNode":[["path",{"d":"M16 3a2 2 0 0 0-2 2v6a2 2 0 0 0 2 2 1 1 0 0 1 1 1v1a2 2 0 0 1-2 2 1 1 0 0 0-1 1v2a1 1 0 0 0 1 1 6 6 0 0 0 6-6V5a2 2 0 0 0-2-2z","key":"rib7q0"}],["path",{"d":"M5 3a2 2 0 0 0-2 2v6a2 2 0 0 0 2 2 1 1 0 0 1 1 1v1a2 2 0 0 1-2 2 1 1 0 0 0-1 1v2a1 1 0 0 0 1 1 6 6 0 0 0 6-6V5a2 2 0 0 0-2-2z","key":"1ymkrd"}]],"className":"lucide-quote absolute -left-8 -top-8 h-16 w-16 text-gold/10 pointer-events-none"}],["$","h2",null,{"className":"font-serif font-bold text-3xl text-navy mb-6","children":"Biography"}],["$","div",null,{"className":"text-navy/80 text-xl leading-relaxed prose prose-navy max-w-none  prose-headings:font-serif prose-headings:font-bold prose-headings:text-navy  prose-h3:text-3xl prose-h3:mt-10 prose-h3:mb-4 prose-a:text-gold hover:prose-a:text-navy prose-a:transition-colors prose-img:rounded-md prose-img:shadow-md prose-img:mx-auto prose-img:border prose-img:border-gold/20 prose-blockquote:border-l-4 prose-blockquote:border-gold prose-blockquote:pl-8  prose-blockquote:italic prose-blockquote:text-navy/80 prose-blockquote:font-serif prose-blockquote:text-2xl prose-blockquote:ml-8 prose-blockquote:my-10 [&_blockquote_p::before]:hidden [&_blockquote_p::after]:hidden","children":[["$","h3","h3-0",{"children":"Introduction"}],"\n",["$","p","p-0",{"children":"David Hamilton Jackson (1884–1946), widely revered as the \"Black Moses\" of the United States Virgin Islands, was a towering figure in the struggle for civil rights, press freedom, and labor justice in the Caribbean. Operating during a critical transitional period in Virgin Islands history—spanning both Danish colonial rule and the early years of American administration—Jackson dedicated his life to dismantling the oppressive structures that disenfranchised the Black working class. Through his fierce journalism, his establishment of the territory's first labor union, and his relentless political advocacy, he fundamentally transformed the socioeconomic landscape of the islands, giving a voice and political agency to the impoverished and marginalized masses."}],"\n",["$","h3","h3-1",{"children":"Early Life in the Danish West Indies"}],"\n",["$","p","p-1",{"children":"Born on September 28, 1884, in Estate East Hill on the island of St. Croix, Jackson grew up in the Danish West Indies—a colonial society defined by deeply entrenched racial and economic inequalities. His father was a local schoolteacher, and his mother was a free Black woman originating from British Antigua. Raised in a household that valued education and critical thinking, Jackson was acutely aware of the systemic injustices surrounding him from a young age."}],"\n",["$","p","p-2",{"children":"In the early 20th century, the Danish West Indies were struggling economically, and the vast majority of the Black population lived in abject poverty. They were bound to the sugar plantations under oppressive labor conditions that barely differed from the era of chattel slavery. Jackson initially followed in his father's footsteps, working as a schoolteacher, an accountant, and a clerk. However, his outspoken nature and his willingness to criticize the colonial administration and the Catholic Church led to frequent clashes with the Danish authorities. He was repeatedly dismissed from his teaching positions for his refusal to remain silent about the inequities he witnessed, experiences that only fueled his commitment to political reform and social justice."}],"\n","$Lb","\n","$Lc","\n","$Ld","\n","$Le","\n","$Lf","\n","$L10","\n","$L11","\n","$L12","\n","$L13","\n","$L14","\n","$L15","\n","$L16","\n","$L17","\n","$L18","\n","$L19"]}]]}],"$L1a","$L1b",false]}],"$L1c"]}]

a:["$","$L1d",null,{"children":["$","$1e",null,{"name":"Next.MetadataOutlet","children":"$@1f"}]}]
b:["$","h3","h3-2",{"children":"The Fight for Freedom of the Press"}]
c:["$","p","p-3",{"children":"One of the most oppressive aspects of Danish colonial rule was a draconian 1779 censorship law that strictly prohibited the publication of independent newspapers. The colonial government maintained a strict monopoly on the press, ensuring that the grievances of the Black majority could never be formally articulated or circulated. Recognizing that an uninformed populace could never successfully mobilize against its oppressors, Jackson decided to take the fight directly to the seat of colonial power."}]
d:["$","p","p-4",{"children":"In 1915, funded by the pennies and small donations of impoverished laborers who believed in his vision, Jackson traveled across the Atlantic to Denmark. There, he petitioned the Danish King and the parliament, demanding the repeal of the censorship laws. His eloquence and unyielding persistence paid off; he successfully secured the repeal of the 1779 edict."}]
e:["$","blockquote","blockquote-0",{"children":["\n",["$","p","p-0",{"children":"\"A people without a voice is a people without power; to speak our truth, we must own the presses that print it.\""}],"\n"]}]
f:["$","p","p-5",{"children":["Returning to St. Croix as a hero, Jackson immediately established ",["$","em","em-0",{"children":"The Herald"}],", the first free and independent newspaper in the history of the Virgin Islands. The inaugural issue was published on November 1, 1915. ",["$","em","em-1",{"children":"The Herald"}]," became a powerful tool for civic education, exposing the horrific working conditions on the plantations and providing a rallying point for the disenfranchised workers."]}]
10:["$","h3","h3-3",{"children":"The Labor Movement and the Great Strike"}]
11:["$","p","p-6",{"children":"Recognizing that political freedom was inextricably linked to economic justice, Jackson co-founded the St. Croix Labor Union in 1915 alongside other early activists. Prior to this, laborers were forced to work from \"sunup to sundown\" for pennies a day, with no legal recourse to demand better conditions. Jackson traveled extensively across the estates of St. Croix, organizing workers and building a formidable coalition capable of challenging the powerful plantocracy."}]
12:["$","p","p-7",{"children":["$","img","img-0",{"src":"https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/7/75/US_Virgin_Islands_in_United_States_%28zoom%29_%28US48%29.svg","alt":"Map of the US Virgin Islands"}]}]
13:["$","p","p-8",{"children":"In January 1916, Jackson led the newly formed union in a historic general strike. Thousands of sugarcane workers across St. Croix refused to work until their demands were met. The strike brought the island's economy to a standstill. Despite threats of violence and severe retaliation from the plantation owners, the workers held their ground. After several tense weeks, the planters capitulated. The strike resulted in a monumental victory: the standard workday was reduced to nine hours, and wages were significantly increased. This watershed moment broke the absolute power of the plantation owners and marked the birth of the modern labor movement in the Virgin Islands."}]
14:["$","h3","h3-4",{"children":"Transfer to US Rule and the Fight for Citizenship"}]
15:["$","p","p-9",{"children":"In 1917, against the backdrop of World War I, Denmark sold the islands to the United States for $25 million, and they were renamed the United States Virgin Islands. While many islanders initially hoped the transfer would bring American democratic ideals and economic prosperity, they soon found themselves under a naval administration that offered them neither the rights of US citizens nor the ability to self-govern."}]
16:["$","p","p-10",{"children":["Jackson, alongside peers like ",["$","$L20","a-0",{"slug":"rothschild-francis","href":"/profiles/rothschild-francis","children":"Rothschild Francis"}],", immediately pivoted his activism to confront the new American administration. He traveled to Washington, D.C., to lobby Congress for full US citizenship for Virgin Islanders, an end to naval rule, and the establishment of a civilian government. Though it would take years of relentless pressure, his advocacy laid the essential groundwork for the eventual passage of the Organic Act of 1936, which granted universal suffrage and civilian rule to the territory."]}]
17:["$","h3","h3-5",{"children":"Later Career and Enduring Legacy"}]
18:["$","p","p-11",{"children":"To better advocate for his people, Jackson later pursued formal legal studies at the University of Chicago and Howard University. Returning to the Virgin Islands as a qualified attorney, he continued to represent laborers and the poor in court. Throughout his later life, he served in various critical public roles, including as a judge, a member of the Colonial Council, and a key political leader until his death on May 30, 1946."}]
19:["$","p","p-12",{"children":["Today, David Hamilton Jackson is remembered as the father of the Virgin Islands civil rights movement. His legacy is officially commemorated every year on November 1st, a public holiday known as \"Liberty Day,\" \"D. Hamilton Jackson Day,\" or \"Bull and Bread Day.\" On this day, Virgin Islanders gather to eat roast beef and bread—a tradition tracing back to the celebratory feast Jackson organized following the launch of ",["$","em","em-0",{"children":"The Herald"}],". Jackson’s life stands as a testament to the power of a single, determined individual to uplift an entire population through courage, organization, and an unwavering commitment to justice."]}]
1a:["$","$L21",null,{"title":"Learn about the legacy of David Hamilton Jackson","url":"https://caribbeanlegacyarchive.com/profiles/hamilton-jackson"}]
1b:["$","div",null,{"className":"mb-12 pt-12 border-t border-gold/10","children":[["$","h2",null,{"className":"font-serif font-bold text-3xl text-navy mb-6","children":"Major Contributions"}],["$","div",null,{"className":"text-navy/80 text-xl leading-relaxed bg-white p-8 border-l-4 border-tropical-green shadow-sm","children":"David Hamilton Jackson's most historic contribution was the successful repeal of the draconian Danish censorship laws in 1915, leading to the establishment of *The Herald*, the first free and independent newspaper in the Virgin Islands. This monumental achievement broke the colonial monopoly on information and gave a powerful voice to the disenfranchised Black majority.\n\nAdditionally, Jackson founded the St. Croix Labor Union and orchestrated the historic 1916 general strike. This action shattered the absolute power of the plantocracy, securing a nine-hour workday and significantly improved wages for sugarcane workers. Following the transfer of the islands to the United States, Jackson became a leading advocate for civil rights, tirelessly lobbying Washington for U.S. citizenship and civilian self-governance for Virgin Islanders, laying the foundation for the modern political structure of the territory."}]]}]
